submission.natural_language_explanation: N942+ fires on the token register of refined, appraised culture: fine art and its display (art, exhibition, gallery, museum, collection, curator, artist, painting, sculpture, architecture), art-historical period/style and connoisseurial appraisal (classical, contemporary, modern, century, Renaissance, cultural, elegance, elegant, exquisite, tasteful, refined, classy, luxury), and upscale design/couture and the refined performing arts (designer, couture, chic, vintage, boutique, decor, master, masterpiece, ballet, opera, theatre, orchestra, symphony, jazz, performance). The trigger is the token, not its sense (art in 'the art of persuasion', master in 'master bedroom' or 'old master', modern in 'modernize', and accented Latin fragments (é, ée, ç) also fire), and it is near-silent outside that register: mass/popular culture (pop, rock, film, movie, television, comics, cartoons, novels, bestsellers), sport, science, nature, medicine, everyday objects and property (bedroom, kitchen, garden, house, car, phone), and plain beauty words (pretty, lovely, beautiful, charming).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The city council approved a plan on Tuesday to convert the old bus depot on Marlowe Street into a public venue, ending four years of argument over the site. The depot, a low brick shed with a leaking roof, has stood empty since the last route moved to the ring road in 2019. Under the plan the building will be cleaned, its roof repaired and its concrete floor leveled, while the tall windows along the northern wall will be reopened.

Funding will come from three sources: a grant from the regional transport fund, money set aside in the capital budget, and a loan the council expects to repay over twenty years. Officials said the transport grant was the hardest to secure, because the fund was set up to pay for bus lanes and cycle tracks rather than buildings. In the end the council argued that the depot sat at the junction of two proposed routes and could serve as a waiting room and ticket office as well as a hall.

Residents raised concerns about parking. The street has room for forty cars at most, and the nearest public car park is a ten minute walk away. Planners replied that the venue would be served by four bus routes and that a covered bike rack would hold sixty bicycles. They also promised to keep the loading bay at the rear for deliveries.

Others asked about noise. The hall will hold up to four hundred people, and the council's environmental health team has set a limit of ninety decibels at the boundary fence. Concerts would have to end by eleven on weeknights, and the organizers would pay for a sound engineer to monitor levels during each event.

The building itself is plain: brick walls below, a steel frame above, a concrete floor, and a ceiling high enough to echo. The trust that will run the venue wants to keep that plainness rather than hide it. Its chair said the aim was to let the shed look like a shed, with new work hung against bare brick and lights run on visible cables. A cafe will open at the front, and the loading bay will become a covered yard for school groups.

A survey of nearby households found that two thirds supported the plan, one fifth opposed it and the rest had no view. The main objection was the loss of the loading bay, which some shops on the street still use for deliveries. The council has promised to keep two spaces at the kerb for that purpose.

Work is due to begin in March and to finish the following autumn. If the timetable holds, the first visitors will walk through the doors two years from now, on a site that has been shut to the public for most of a decade.

On the upper floor, behind a row of small windows, the trust plans to open a contemporary art gallery, with a permanent collection of prints and a changing exhibition of sculpture.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The marathon begins long before the starting gun. Runners spend sixteen weeks building distance, adding a few miles each Sunday until the long run reaches twenty, then easing back while the legs recover. Coaches argue about pace, shoes and sleep, but the basics change little: eat, run, rest, repeat.

On race morning the roads close at five. Volunteers set out water cups on folding tables and chalk arrows at every turn. The first wave leaves at six, the second at six twenty, and the last at seven, when the sun is already high over the river. Spectators gather on the bridge with signs and cowbells, shouting the names printed on shirts.

The route runs east along the river, turns north through the old market district, and climbs for two miles before dropping back to the water. The climb is the hardest stretch. Runners who go out too fast on the flat pay for it there, and the medical tent at the top fills quickly with cramp and nausea. Volunteers hand out bananas, salt tablets and bandages.

By noon the leaders are finishing. The winner crosses in two hours eleven, a minute clear of the second, and collapses into the arms of two helpers. Behind him the field strings out for miles: club runners chasing a personal best, charity runners in fancy dress, walkers who started at seven and will finish after the streets reopen. The sweep bus follows the last of them, collecting anyone who cannot go on.

Results are posted on a board beside the finish. Runners crowd around it, phones out, comparing times with friends. Some are pleased, some are not. A man in a blue vest finds his name, stares at the number, and walks away without a word. His training partner finished four minutes ahead.

The organisers spend the afternoon clearing the course. They pick up cups, fold the tables, take down the banners and count the leftover medals. A crew drives the length of the route in a van, checking that no signs remain and that the road sweeper has passed. By evening the streets look as they did the day before.

Volunteers arrive even earlier than the runners. The same families have worked the water station at mile eight for a decade, and they know most of the regulars by name. They bring thermoses, folding chairs and a radio, and they stay until the sweep bus passes, long after the elite runners have gone home.

Entry for next year opens in a month. The organisers expect thirty thousand places to fill within a week, as they have every year since the race began. They will keep the same route, the same start time and the same climb, because the runners complained about it, and then entered again.
